notes.meaning: Jehoram became king over the northern kingdom of Israel while Jehoshaphat was ruling Judah. He was Ahab's son and took the throne after his brother Ahaziah died without having any children. He made his royal home in Samaria and ruled there for twelve years.

Jehoram was an evil ruler, but he did not go as far into idolatry—the worship of false gods—as his parents Ahab and Jezebel. He removed the stone pillar dedicated to the false god Baal that his father had made. Even so, he merely set it aside rather than destroying it completely or turning the hearts of his people back to the Lord.

Jehoram continued to lead Israel in the worship of golden calf statues started long ago by King Jeroboam. Jeroboam had set up those idols as a political trick to stop the northern tribes from traveling south to worship at the temple in Jerusalem. Jehoram refused to abandon these idols because he believed keeping them protected his own royal power.

King Mesha of Moab ruled a country known for rich grazing lands and owned vast herds of sheep. As a conquered ruler serving Israel, he was forced to pay an enormous yearly tax of one hundred thousand lambs and the wool of one hundred thousand rams. This heavy tribute formed a major part of the northern king's wealth.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: In 1868, an ancient stone monument known as the Mesha Stele was discovered, on which King Mesha wrote his own account of being oppressed by the kings of Israel before he rebelled.

notes.meaning: As soon as King Ahab died, the king of Moab broke his agreement and stopped sending the yearly tribute. Israel's next king, Ahaziah, had been too weak and sickly to fight back. Now that Jehoram held the throne, he was eager to put down the rebellion and win that wealth back.
Jehoram marched out of his capital city of Samaria and gathered every fighting man in Israel. He wanted to make sure his army was large enough to bring Moab back under control.

Jehoram sent messengers asking godly King Jehoshaphat of Judah to join him in the war against Moab. Jehoshaphat quickly promised his support, offering his own soldiers and horses for the fight. Jehoshaphat was willing to help an ungodly king, using the very same words of partnership he had once spoken to Jehoram's father Ahab.

The kings planned their route and chose to march through the harsh southern desert of Edom. This path took them around the southern tip of the Dead Sea, which was a longer journey but allowed them to add Edom's soldiers to their ranks. It also let them attack Moab's border where the defenses were weakest.

The three allied kings marched their massive armies through the rugged wilderness for seven days. When they reached the dry valley where they hoped to find a stream, there was no water left. Soon both the soldiers and their pack animals were on the verge of dying from severe thirst.

Jehoram gave in to terror and blamed God for the disaster. He complained that the Lord had brought the three kings together only to let Moab slaughter them. Instead of seeing his own lack of wisdom, he accused God of cruelty.

Jehoshaphat responded to the crisis by asking if a true prophet of the Lord was nearby so they could seek God's counsel. An officer from Israel reported that Elisha was traveling with the army. The servant identified Elisha as the faithful man who had served Elijah by washing his hands.

Jehoshaphat recognized that Elisha was a genuine speaker of God's truth. Instead of demanding that the prophet come before their royal court, all three kings showed deep respect and went down to Elisha's tent. Trouble had finally humbled these rulers enough to seek God's servant in person.

Elisha gave King Jehoram a sharp and stinging rebuke. He told the king to go ask help from the false prophets supported by his father and mother. Jehoram answered humbly, pleading that all three kings and their armies would perish if God did not rescue them.

Elisha swore by the living Lord of Hosts that he would have refused even to look at wicked Jehoram. The only reason he agreed to help was his deep respect for godly King Jehoshaphat of Judah. Often ungodly people are spared from ruin simply because they are in the company of those who love God.

Elisha called for a musician to play sacred music on a harp. His heart had been stirred with anger by the sight of Jehoram, and the peaceful music helped calm his emotions and quiet his thoughts. As the harp was played, the power of the Holy Spirit came upon Elisha to deliver God's answer.

God commanded the soldiers to dig trenches and pits throughout the dry valley. These ditches were needed to hold the water God was preparing to send so that it would not wash away. The men had to act in faith and do hard work before they could see any visible sign of relief.

God promised that the valley would soon be filled with water, even though the soldiers would see no rain clouds and feel no storm winds. There would be plenty of water for all the men, their cattle, and their pack animals to drink. The Lord can meet the needs of His people in quiet ways that go beyond ordinary human expectations.

Elisha told them that filling the dry valley with water was an easy thing for the Lord to do. Beyond providing water, God was also going to hand the entire army of Moab over to them. The Lord often gives far greater blessings than the ones His people originally asked to receive.

Elisha announced that the allied armies would capture Moab's fortified cities and tear down its defenses. They would also chop down its best trees, plug up every fresh spring, and cover the productive fields with stones. This was a severe judgment against a cruel nation in open rebellion.

At the exact hour of the morning sacrifice at the temple in Jerusalem, water suddenly rushed into the valley from the hills of Edom. God had caused a heavy rainstorm far away in the distant mountains during the night. The water filled every ditch the soldiers had dug, showing that God honored the hour of prayer and worship.

When the Moabites heard that three kings were marching to invade their land, they called up every male old enough to put on armor. They lined up their combined forces along the southern border, ready to defend their homeland from attack.

The Moabites looked across the valley early in the morning just as the sun rose over the hills. The low morning sunlight shone across the pools of water and made the trenches appear bright red. Because they knew the valley was normally bone-dry and had seen no rain, they mistook the red reflection for pools of blood.

The Moabite soldiers shouted that the three allied kings must have fought and destroyed one another during the night. Thinking the camp was full of corpses and abandoned riches, they threw away all order and rushed ahead to plunder the tents. Their foolish greed led them straight toward their own defeat.

When the disorganized Moabites reached the camp, the refreshed Israelite soldiers sprang up and attacked them with full force. The Moabite army broke and ran away in panic. The Israelites pursued them across the border and struck down their enemies inside their own land.

The Israelites swept through Moab, tearing down cities, filling good fields with stones, blocking fresh springs, and cutting down fruit trees. Only the royal stronghold of Kir-haraseth was left standing, but soldiers armed with slings surrounded the fortress and showered the walls with stones.

Seeing that his stronghold was about to fall, the king of Moab gathered seven hundred skilled swordsmen for a desperate counterattack. He tried to break through the lines held by the king of Edom, thinking that was the weakest part of the siege. The defenders held their ground firmly, and the Moabite king was driven back inside the fortress.

In utter desperation, the king of Moab took his oldest son, who was set to rule after him, and burned him as a human sacrifice on top of the city wall to please his false god Chemosh. This gruesome act filled everyone with horror, and great distress and anger fell on Israel for driving the war to such a savage extreme. The allied armies broke camp and returned home.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: In ancient Near Eastern warfare, offering the crown prince was seen as a final, desperate ritual meant to force a god to save a city under siege.
